name: Honey and ginger throat soothing

lead: Honey and ginger in warm drinks are used to soothe a sore throat and keep the voice comfortable and easy to use.

Proponents say honey coats the throat and ginger soothes it. A Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found no strong evidence for or against honey for coughs, while the WHO recommends honey for coughs and sore throats. Ginger has a long traditional-medicine history, and its effectiveness for treating disease remains uncertain.

paras: People stir honey, fresh ginger or both into hot water or tea, usually when the throat feels rough or after heavy voice use.
Honey should not be given to infants under one because of infant botulism risk. Ginger can interact with anticoagulants.

angle.text: Honey and ginger drinks soothe a sore, irritated throat so the voice feels easier and clearer. Honey has some cough data and WHO guidance for sore throats, while ginger rests on traditional use.

lead: Honey and ginger throat soothing is a folk remedy in which honey, ginger or both are taken in warm drinks or teas to ease a scratchy, sore or hoarse throat. People reach for it to keep the voice sounding clear and comfortable, which matters for anyone who speaks, sings or performs and wants their voice to come across well.

Honey is the better-studied half. A Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found no strong evidence either way for honey in adult coughs, while for children there is moderate to low-quality evidence that it reduces coughing more than no treatment or placebo. The World Health Organization recommends honey for coughs and sore throats, and the UK MHRA suggests honey and lemon as a safer option than over-the-counter cough medicine for children under six.[1]

Ginger has been used for centuries in Chinese, Indian and Japanese traditional medicine, and its pungent compounds are mainly gingerols and shogaols.[2] Wikipedia describes some evidence of an anti-inflammatory effect and says it remains uncertain whether ginger is effective for treating any disease.[2] Honey is not recommended for infants under one year because of infant botulism risk.[1]

paras: Evidence for honey easing children's cough is described as moderate to low quality. The UK MHRA suggests honey and lemon as a safer option than over-the-counter cough medicine for children under six, and the WHO recommends honey for coughs and sore throats, including in children.[1] A Cochrane review found no strong evidence either way for adult coughs.[1] Honey is not recommended before age one because of infant botulism risk.[1]
Wikipedia also reports early evidence that honey heals partial-thickness burns faster than some dressings, which is a separate use from throat comfort.[1]

Ginger's aroma and bite come mainly from volatile oils, gingerols, shogaols and zingerone, with -gingerol the main pungent compound.[2] Some evidence suggests an anti-inflammatory effect, though Wikipedia says it is not sufficient to show ginger relieves osteoarthritis pain, and it remains uncertain whether ginger treats any disease.[2]
Ginger is generally recognised as safe by the FDA; large amounts can cause heartburn or digestive discomfort, and it may interact with anticoagulants such as warfarin, aspirin and nifedipine.[2]

The UK NHS's sore throat page lists gargling warm salty water, drinking plenty of water, eating cool or soft foods, avoiding smoke, sucking ice cubes or lozenges and resting; it does not mention honey or warm drinks.[3]

Remedies for singers and speakers come up in a T Nation thread on home remedies, where a poster mentions the herbal supplement slippery elm as something that soothes the throat so people who make a living with their voice can perform when sick.[4]

No studies found on honey and ginger for voice quality or vocal strain specifically; honey studies cover cough in general.[1] A Cochrane review found no strong evidence either way for honey in adult coughs, while evidence in children is moderate to low quality.[1]
